comments.text: Thank you! And: there are a few additional points worth making. First: many durable assets are inflated by artificial scarcity; chief among them are HOMES. When a house-price rises, the house itself did NOT improve in quality or value-creation in real, material terms; it only became rarer, such that you need more dollars to buy one, which is fundamentally a devaluation of dollars. When investors list assets, and those assets see inflated dollar-values without the underlying asset improving, then that can ONLY be balanced by either current-inflation or future-inflation; the dollar MUST decline in value to compensate for that 'rising asset class.' Second: the holder of the loan, collecting interest, lists that loan-promise as an asset, even if global conditions might wipe-out real productivity, triggering a default on that loan; loans are valued as assets under present-conditions expectations. So, when a borrower takes a loan and burns the money, then the debt is still listed as an asset even though the global economy lost dollars; they just don't find out that they are broken until the bubble pops. Finally: regardless of all the financials, regardless of bonds or valuations or expected yields, there is only ONE real value - the tangible value. When a country stops producting real products which themselves generate real, material value, then they MUST see a decline in total assets, either through recession or inflation. This means that when America switched from building factories and homes, toward producing cute hand-bags, hotel services, and meme-shows, then America built-in real, material decline by producing less real, material value. The only things which have real value are those which produce real value; skills and machines. Everything else is smoke and mirrors.
